culture.summary: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. culture.title: Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?
culture.summary: Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world . On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg). People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi. Continue reading...

culture.title: Tom yum party mix, chicory boats and peanut sprout skewers: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for Christmas canapés
culture.summary: A Christmas party mix of moreishy savoury, spicy, salty and citrussy bites to suit every palate. Just add a glass or three of fizz Party food should be about maximum pleasure and minimum fuss. It should feel generous, delicious, easy to eat, and simple enough to put together, not least so the host can enjoy the festivities, too. ’Tis the season for crunchy, salty snacks such as my dangerously addictive tom yum party mix that can be scarfed by the fistful, a refreshing citrus salad piled up on the best edible vessel, namely chicory, and sprouts on sticks with peanut sauce that can be passed around. Importantly, all of these leave one hand free for a glass of something deliciously festive. Happy Christmas everyone! Continue reading...

culture.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
culture.summary: Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases. According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK , fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard. Continue reading...

culture.title: ‘Opposites don’t attract’: Adam Grant on how to strengthen friendships and make new ones faster
culture.summary: The organisational psychologist and bestselling author says learning about the four types of platonic bonds can help us understand our relationships Here’s a stat to ruin your day: of all the people you would call a friend, research suggests only about half would reciprocate. The thought might make you want to wipe your contacts list and start afresh. But let’s look on the positive side, suggests Adam Grant, the Wharton organisational psychologist and New York Times bestselling author of Originals, and Hidden Potential. Continue reading...

culture.title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help
culture.summary: About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions. That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years. Continue reading...

culture.title: She gets 16 pelvic exams a day – so yours don’t hurt
culture.summary: Molly Callahan, a gynecological teaching assistant, helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams On her busiest days, Molly Callahan, has 16 speculums inserted into her vagina. She works full-time as a gynecological teaching assistant ( GTA ) – a layperson who helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams before they work with actual patients. It’s not as unpleasant as you might think. In fact, the point is to help students learn how to do it without causing discomfort. Contrary to common belief, pap smears – tests that screen for cervical cancer – don’t have to be painful. Continue reading...

politics.title: Unpaid TV licence or cycling on pavement could bar people from settling in UK

Under the plans, which are to come into effect next year, securing indefinite leave to remain will become significantly harder for many people. The rules introduce a strict new threshold where any adult conviction resulting in a court disposal – including fines, community orders, conditional cautions, and absolute or conditional discharges – triggers mandatory refusal. politics.title: They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson | Robert Hutton
politics.summary: He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works? What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays. But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else? Continue reading...

entertainment.title: ‘Who asked that? You should be ashamed of yourself!’: Judi Dench answers questions from Ian McKellen, Lorraine Kelly, David Hare and more
entertainment.summary: Fans and famous friends put their nosiest questions to the 91-year-old actor It’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. It’s one of the smallest rooms in her Elizabethan home: timber beams, terracotta-painted walls, her father’s consulting-room desk and chair within touching distance, together with the bronze “Dr Dench” plaque that used to hang on the railings outside their family home in York. Behind Judi’s head hangs an enormous painting of her as M, presented as a gift on her last day of filming on Skyfall . Through the latticed windows is a view on to the garden, which is crowded with trees she plants for lost friends and family – a beloved oak, a tribute to her late husband, actor Michael Williams, towers above the pond. Even though the room is suffused with autumn sunshine, all the lights are on in the house. Judi has always needed light around her – she’s been afraid of the dark since she was small. Continue reading...

entertainment.title: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
entertainment.summary: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’” In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches. entertainment.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
entertainment.summary: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!” Continue reading...

entertainment.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack
entertainment.summary: (Atlantic) Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits. entertainment.title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
entertainment.summary: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

entertainment.title: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy
entertainment.summary: Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi . Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. Continue reading...

entertainment.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
entertainment.summary: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).
